questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines an IAM role, as distinguished from the other identities Chapter 1 covers?
options: An identity with permission policies that is assumed temporarily through STS, with no permanent password or access keys of its own
A named individual identity with its own console password and/or long-lived access keys, starting with zero permissions by default
A JSON document that spells out exactly what's allowed or denied for a user or group
The identity tied to the account's sign-up email, with unrestricted, unremovable access to everything in the account
A named collection of IAM users that share permissions attached to the collection itself
A policy attached to an Organizational Unit that sets the maximum permissions available to every account under it
questions.explain: An IAM role has permission policies attached to it like a user, but it has no password and no permanent access keys — it's assumed by a trusted entity (a user, an application, or an AWS service like EC2), and AWS STS issues temporary credentials that expire on their own, no manual cleanup required.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes an IAM user, not a role — a user is a named identity with its own long-lived credentials and zero permissions by default, while a role is never owned permanently by anyone and never carries a password. Confusing the two is exactly why Lesson 3 spends a whole lesson on the EC2-instance-reading-S3 example.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 1, which of these actually requires signing in as the AWS root user rather than an IAM administrator user?
options: Closing the AWS account entirely
Launching an EC2 instance
Creating an S3 bucket
Writing an IAM policy that grants least-privilege access
questions.explain: Lesson 1's real, short list of root-only actions includes closing the account entirely, changing root's own email or password, viewing certain billing/tax documents, changing the Support plan, and restoring a locked-out IAM user's permissions. Everything else — launching servers, managing storage, writing IAM policies — belongs to the IAM administrator user created in the standard setup sequence.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 term to what it actually means.
right: The identity created with the AWS account itself, tied to the sign-up email, with unrestricted access to everything
A named collection of IAM users that share permissions attached to the group itself
The document on an IAM role that defines exactly who or what is allowed to assume it
A container that groups accounts (or other OUs) into a hierarchy under the Organization's root
questions.explain: Root is the unremovable, unrestricted identity born with the account. A group attaches permissions once for everyone inside it. A trust policy is what actually gates who can assume a role. An OU is how AWS Organizations builds a hierarchy out of a flat list of member accounts.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Service Control Policy (SCP) sets the ________ permissions available to every account under it, including that account's own root user, overriding anything any IAM policy inside the account would otherwise allow.
questions.explain: An SCP is a ceiling, not a grant — unlike an IAM policy, which grants permissions, an SCP only restricts what's possible in the first place, and that ceiling applies even to an account's own root user, which is exactly what makes it different from every other access control covered so far.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes stopping an EC2 instance from terminating it?
options: Stop powers the instance off but preserves the root EBS volume, so compute billing stops while storage billing continues; terminate permanently deletes the instance and, by default, deletes the root EBS volume too
Stop permanently deletes the instance and its root volume, while terminate merely powers the instance off
Both stop and terminate delete the root EBS volume by default, with no way to prevent it
Stop requires capturing a new AMI first; terminate does not require anything beforehand
Instance store volumes survive a stop the same way the root EBS volume does
Stop and terminate are simply two names for exactly the same action
questions.explain: Stopping preserves the root EBS volume — you can start the same instance ID again later, exactly as you left it — while terminating is permanent, and by default also deletes the root volume via its DeleteOnTermination flag (set to false beforehand if you need the disk to survive). Any instance-store volumes, by contrast, are wiped on a stop because the instance may restart on different hardware.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two mechanics entirely backwards — it's terminate that's permanent and deletes the root volume by default, while stop is the reversible one that preserves it. Getting this backwards is precisely the mistake Lesson 6 warns can cost you real data.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about EC2 instance families, per Lesson 7.
options: T-series instances accumulate CPU credits while idle and spend them to burst above baseline for short periods
C-series has a high vCPU-to-memory ratio, suited to CPU-bound workloads like batch processing or video encoding
R-series is memory-optimized, suited to in-memory caches and large relational databases
M-series is the burstable, credit-based family that throttles back to baseline once its credits run out
A T-series instance running sustained high CPU will exhaust its credit balance and get throttled back to baseline
questions.explain: T-series is the burstable family with CPU credits, not M-series — M-series is balanced general purpose with steady, non-bursting performance. C-series trades memory for raw CPU, and R-series trades the reverse, trading CPU for memory headroom. A T-series instance that sustains high CPU for too long burns through its credit balance and gets throttled back to baseline, which is exactly why it fits spiky, low-average workloads and not steady production ones.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on an EC2 instance type name like c6g.xlarge, the optional capability letter 'g' indicates the instance uses an AWS ________ (ARM) processor.
questions.explain: Reading c6g.xlarge in order — compute-optimized family, 6th generation, Graviton (ARM) processor, xlarge size — is exactly the skill Lesson 7 builds: the capability letter tells you when an instance departs from the standard Intel chip, with 'g' marking AWS's own Graviton processors.

questions.prompt: Put the five decisions every EC2 launch requires, per Lesson 5, in the order they're listed.
items: Choose the AMI (operating system and pre-installed software)
Choose the instance type (CPU, memory, and network performance)
Choose the network (which VPC and subnet)
Choose storage (the root EBS volume size and type, plus any extra volumes)
Choose the key pair and security group (how you'll authenticate and what traffic is allowed in)
questions.explain: Lesson 5 frames a `run-instances` call as a checklist rather than a wall of flags: what OS, how much hardware, where on the network, how much disk, and finally how you'll get in and what's allowed to reach it — in that order, each decision building on a clear picture of what the instance needs to do.

questions.prompt: A file is read and written constantly throughout the day. Per Lesson 9, which S3 storage class actually fits, and why would S3 Standard-IA be the wrong pick?
options: S3 Standard — Standard-IA charges a per-GB retrieval fee every time the object is actually read, which erases its lower storage cost the moment access is frequent rather than rare
S3 Glacier — the cheapest storage class is always the right choice regardless of access pattern
S3 Standard-IA — its lower storage cost always wins no matter how often the data is read
S3 Standard-IA, because it offers faster retrieval than S3 Standard
questions.explain: S3 Standard-IA trades a lower storage cost for a per-GB retrieval fee charged on every read — a reasonable trade for data you rarely touch, but a losing one for data accessed constantly, where those retrieval fees stack up and erase the storage savings. S3 Standard is the default precisely because it's built for data read or written regularly, with no retrieval fee at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about S3 versioning, lifecycle rules, and access control, per Lesson 10.
options: Enabling versioning means a plain DELETE adds a delete marker instead of destroying the object outright
A lifecycle rule can target noncurrent versions specifically, so old versions don't quietly pile up and cost money forever
S3 Block Public Access overrides a bucket policy or ACL that would otherwise make a bucket public
Bucket policies are identity-based policies attached to a user or role, the same as IAM policies
Once versioning is enabled, every PUT to an existing key permanently overwrites the prior version
questions.explain: Versioning turns a delete into a reversible delete marker rather than real destruction, and a lifecycle rule pairs naturally with it by aging out noncurrent versions before they pile up. S3 Block Public Access exists specifically to override an accidentally public policy or ACL. Bucket policies are resource-based, attached to the bucket itself, not identity-based like IAM policies — and once versioning is on, a PUT to an existing key creates a new version rather than overwriting the old one.

questions.prompt: Match each storage term from Lessons 11-12 to what it actually is.
right: General Purpose SSD delivering a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of volume size
Provisioned IOPS SSD for high-IOPS, low-latency workloads, with a higher durability guarantee than gp3
A point-in-time, incremental backup of a volume, stored behind the scenes in S3
The rule that an EBS volume must live in the same AZ as the instance it attaches to
questions.explain: gp3 is the default general-purpose SSD with baseline performance independent of size; io2 is reserved for demanding, low-latency workloads at higher durability. A snapshot is an incremental, point-in-time backup stored in S3 behind the scenes. And an EBS volume's AZ binding is the reason you snapshot-and-recreate rather than directly reattach across AZs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an EBS snapshot's first copy captures every block, but every snapshot after that only copies the blocks that ________ since the last snapshot.
questions.explain: The incremental design is why a nightly snapshot schedule stays cheap over time — only the delta since the last snapshot is persisted, even though each snapshot still represents the volume's complete state at that moment when you restore from it.

questions.prompt: An administrator carves a /28 subnet (16 addresses total) out of a VPC. Per Lesson 13, how many usable addresses does that subnet actually end up with?
options: 11 — AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet regardless of size
16, because very small subnets are exempt from the reserved-address rule
6, because a /28 loses twice as many reserved addresses as a /24 does
0, because a /28 is too small for AWS to provision resources into at all
questions.explain: AWS reserves exactly 5 addresses in every subnet it provisions — network address, VPC router, two for DNS/future use, and broadcast — no matter the subnet's size. A /24 barely notices losing 5 out of 256, but a /28's 16 total addresses drop to 11 usable, which is exactly the detail Lesson 13 flags before anyone sizes a small subnet for something that still needs room to grow.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Internet Gateways and NAT Gateways, per Lessons 14-15.
options: A subnet becomes public purely because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an Internet Gateway, not because of a literal setting
An instance in a subnet with a route to an Internet Gateway is automatically reachable from the internet even without a public IP
A NAT Gateway lets private-subnet instances start outbound connections while remaining unreachable from the internet side
A NAT Gateway must live in a public subnet, not the private subnet it actually serves
Every VPC route table's local route for the VPC's own CIDR block can be edited or deleted
questions.explain: Public is purely a routing fact, not a flag AWS exposes directly. A route to an IGW alone isn't enough — the instance still needs its own public IP to be reachable. A NAT Gateway solves the opposite problem: outbound-only access for a private subnet, placed in a public subnet with an Elastic IP, never accepting unsolicited inbound traffic. The VPC's local route, by contrast, is automatic and permanent — you can add routes alongside it, but you can't touch it.

questions.prompt: Match each networking component from Chapter 4 to what it actually does.
right: Stateful, instance-level firewall; allow-only rules, inbound denied by default
Stateless, subnet-level firewall; numbered allow/deny rules evaluated in ascending order, first match wins
VPC component that enables internet connectivity and performs NAT for instances with public IPs
AWS-managed gateway, placed in a public subnet, giving private-subnet instances outbound-only internet access
questions.explain: A Security Group filters per instance and auto-allows return traffic; a Network ACL filters per subnet and needs explicit rules in both directions because it's stateless. An Internet Gateway is what a public route actually points at, while a NAT Gateway gives a private subnet outbound-only access without ever becoming reachable from the internet side.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for making a subnet serve internet-bound public traffic, per Lesson 14, in the correct order.
items: Attach the Internet Gateway to the VPC
Create a route sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway in the subnet's route table
Enable map-public-ip-on-launch so new instances get a public IP automatically
questions.explain: Creating an IGW does nothing until it's attached to a VPC, and attaching it does nothing until a route table actually points traffic at it. Even then, a route alone only gets an instance out to the internet — map-public-ip-on-launch is the separate setting that makes an instance reachable back, which is exactly the step Lesson 14 warns is easy to forget.

questions.prompt: A named profile is created with `aws configure --profile prod`. Per Lesson 17, how does that profile's section header actually differ between ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config?
options: It's `[prod]` in credentials but `[profile prod]` in config
It's `[profile prod]` in both files
It's `[prod]` in both files
It's `[default]` in config and `[prod]` in credentials
questions.explain: Every profile section in ~/.aws/config except `default` gets a literal `profile` prefix, while the same profile's section in ~/.aws/credentials is just the bare name. That mismatch is the exact detail Lesson 17 flags as the thing that trips up almost everyone the first time they troubleshoot a profile that isn't working.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: `aws ec2 describe-instances --output ________` strips the formatting down to tab-separated values — the output format a shell script loops over line by line.
questions.explain: Of the three output formats Lesson 18 covers, `table` is for reading results interactively, `json` is the full-detail default that `--query` operates against, and `text` is specifically the stripped-down, scriptable format behind Lesson 19's CloudShell loop.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AWS CloudShell, per Lesson 19.
options: CloudShell is pre-authenticated, inheriting the same IAM permissions as the console user who launched it
CloudShell requires running `aws configure` before first use, same as a fresh local terminal
CloudShell gives each user 1 GB of persistent storage per AWS Region that survives between sessions
CloudShell is the right tool for long-running or scheduled automation
The AWS CLI and Python come pre-installed in CloudShell
questions.explain: CloudShell's two genuinely useful properties are being pre-authenticated (no `aws configure` step at all) and pre-installed (CLI, Python, and other tools already there), plus 1 GB of persistent storage per Region. It's explicitly the wrong tool for scheduled or long-running automation — that job belongs in Lambda or a CI/CD pipeline instead.

questions.prompt: A company applies a new `CostCenter` tag to its EC2 instances and activates it as a Cost Allocation Tag in AWS Billing the same day. Per Lesson 20, when can they expect to see spend broken out by that tag in Cost Explorer?
options: Not for up to 24 hours after activation
Instantly, the moment the tag is applied to a resource
Only at the very start of the next calendar month
Tags never appear broken out in Cost Explorer, only in the resource list in the console
questions.explain: A user-defined tag has to be manually activated as a Cost Allocation Tag in AWS Billing before it shows up as its own line at all, and even after activation it can take up to 24 hours for tagged costs to start appearing split out — a detail that catches anyone expecting same-day results.

questions.prompt: An EC2 instance has been running for a week. CloudWatch shows CPUUtilization and NetworkIn/NetworkOut automatically, but never reports free memory. Per Lesson 21, why not, and what actually fixes it?
options: Default platform metrics come from the hypervisor watching from outside the guest OS; installing the CloudWatch Agent inside the OS is what reports memory
Memory metrics are a paid add-on with no way to enable them on EC2
Turning on detailed monitoring automatically starts reporting memory usage
Memory usage is reported automatically once an instance has been running for more than a week
questions.explain: CPUUtilization and network metrics are free and automatic because the hypervisor can see them from outside the instance — but memory usage and free disk space happen entirely inside the guest OS, which the hypervisor can't see into. Only something running inside the OS, the CloudWatch Agent, can close that gap, and detailed monitoring only changes the interval of existing metrics, not which ones are reported.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about CloudWatch Alarms, per Lesson 22.
options: An alarm can be in one of three states: OK, ALARM, or INSUFFICIENT_DATA
Only the transition into ALARM actually fires the notification, not every period it continues to stay there
An alarm sends email or SMS directly to a recipient, with no need for SNS
A brand-new SNS email subscription sits in 'pending confirmation' until the subscriber clicks the confirmation link
INSUFFICIENT_DATA means the metric has definitely breached its configured threshold
questions.explain: An alarm's three real states are OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA — the last one simply meaning CloudWatch hasn't received enough data points yet, not a breach. An alarm never notifies directly; it publishes to an SNS topic, and a fresh email or SMS subscription sits unconfirmed until the subscriber clicks the link AWS sends — meaning the alarm can fire all day while that subscriber hears nothing.

questions.prompt: Match each CloudWatch Logs term from Lesson 23 to what it actually is.
right: The top-level container for related log streams, with its own retention setting
A sequence of log events from one specific source inside a log group
Software installed inside an instance's OS to ship its logs (and OS-level metrics) to CloudWatch
The query language for searching log data that's already flowing into CloudWatch Logs
questions.explain: A log group is the per-application or per-resource-type container, with a log stream underneath it per individual source. Neither exists for an EC2 instance's own OS logs without the CloudWatch Agent shipping them there, and once they're flowing, Logs Insights is how you search across every stream in a group at once.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: CloudTrail's always-on Event History records the last ________ days of account activity automatically, at no extra charge.
questions.explain: Event History is enabled for every AWS account with zero setup, covering the last 90 days — enough for most 'who did this?' questions on a recent incident. Anything beyond that window, or delivery to S3 for longer retention, requires configuring a Trail instead.

questions.prompt: A monthly AWS bill jumps unexpectedly from its usual level. Per Lesson 25, what's the right first move in Cost Explorer to trace the actual cause?
options: Group the current month's spend by service first, then filter to the top service and group that by tag
Open and read every invoice line item by hand
Wait for Cost Explorer's forecast to explain the spike automatically
Delete the most recently launched resource and see whether the bill drops
questions.explain: Lesson 25's worked example goes from 'the bill is high' to 'a specific project's EC2 usage is the reason' in two clicks: group by service to find what's driving the increase, then filter to that service and group by tag to find which project or team it belongs to — no invoice line-reading required.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AWS Budgets and EC2 pricing models, per Lessons 26 and 28.
options: An AWS Budget crossing 100% does not stop, throttle, or block any resource on its own
A forecasted-spend alert threshold can fire before actual spend has crossed anything, based on pace so far
A Reserved Instance is a 1- or 3-year commitment to a specific instance family in a specific Region for a discount
Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS with a short notice period, commonly a two-minute warning
A usage budget tracks spend in dollars, exactly the same as a cost budget
questions.explain: A budget is strictly a watchdog, never a brake — crossing 100% only fires a notification. A forecasted-spend threshold is the earlier warning, projecting ahead of actual spend. Reserved Instances trade a 1- or 3-year commitment for a discount, and Spot Instances trade reclaimability (a two-minute warning) for steep savings. A usage budget tracks a quantity of usage like instance-hours, not dollars — that's what a cost budget does instead.

questions.prompt: Put these right-sizing steps from Lesson 27 in the correct order.
items: Check CloudWatch CPUUtilization and memory metrics averaged over a couple of weeks
Identify an instance that never breaks 10-15% CPU as a downsize candidate
Change the instance type to a smaller size in the same family
questions.explain: Right-sizing starts with evidence, not a guess — a couple of weeks of CloudWatch data identifying a consistently underused instance — and only then moves to the actual mechanics: stop, change the instance type down within the same family, and start again, exactly the sequence Lesson 27's m5.xlarge-to-m5.large example walks through.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, as introduced in Lesson 31's troubleshooting case study?
options: A service that provides shell access to an instance without SSH, an open port 22, or a public IP, working over the AWS API
A tool that automatically detects and fixes a misconfigured subnet route table
A CloudWatch feature that alerts whenever an instance loses its public IP address
A type of IAM role created specifically for EC2 instances
A Regional service dedicated to creating VPC peering connections
A CLI command that lists every orphaned EBS volume in an account
questions.explain: After fixing meridian-web2's wrong-subnet problem, Lesson 31 notes Meridian's ops team moves to Session Manager for admin access going forward — it works over the AWS API with no open port 22 and no public IP required, removing the entire category of reachability mistake the case study just walked through.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes an automated remediation tool, which Session Manager isn't — it's a connectivity mechanism for getting a shell on an instance, not something that inspects or repairs route tables on its own. Treating a connectivity tool as an auto-fix tool is exactly the kind of confusion this lesson's case study is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the Meridian case study, meridian-web2 had no public IP because the ops team copy-pasted the wrong ________ ID, placing the instance in the private subnet instead of the public one.
questions.explain: Lesson 31's four-question diagnostic sequence traced the problem to `describe-instances` reporting SubnetId as `subnet-0meridianpriv` — the app tier's subnet, copy-pasted from old shell history instead of the public subnet meant for a second web-tier instance. An EC2 instance can't be moved between subnets after launch, so the fix was to terminate and relaunch it into the correct subnet.

questions.prompt: Put these four stages of the Meridian capstone, per Lesson 32's review, in the order Lessons 29-32 actually ran them.
items: Deploy the VPC, subnets, and EC2 instances for the web and app tiers
Scope security groups, attach an IAM role, and set a CloudWatch alarm
Diagnose and fix the unreachable meridian-web2 instance
Review how identity, compute, storage, networking, the CLI, and monitoring combined across the whole course
questions.explain: Lesson 32 walks back through exactly this order: Lesson 29 stood the environment up, Lesson 30 secured and monitored it, Lesson 31 diagnosed a real incident using the same CLI skills from Chapter 5, and Lesson 32 itself is the step back to see how every earlier chapter's subject matter — identity, compute, storage, networking, the CLI, and monitoring — combined into one administered environment rather than four separate topics.
